title: The Camel Race Champion
summary: A girl trains her family's racing camel for a traditional regional race and learns that patience and proper care, not speed alone, are what truly make a champion.
poll: A winning racing camel is simply born fast, and training cannot change that.

versions.title: The Camel Race Champion
versions.text:
Lama's family had camels. She had a young camel. Its name was Najma. Lama wanted to win a race.

Lama trained Najma each day. She made Najma run fast. She did not let her rest. She just wanted speed.

Soon, Najma got tired. She did not eat well. She did not want to run.

Lama's grandpa saw this. He said speed is not all. A champion needs patience too. A champion needs good care.

Lama heard him. She gave Najma good food. She let her rest a lot. She was slow and kind with her.

Soon, Najma felt strong. She felt well. She liked Lama more.

On race day, Najma ran well. She was fast. She was strong. Lama saw that care and patience make a true champion.

versions.title: The Camel Race Champion
versions.text:
Lama's family had raised camels for many years. She had a young camel named Najma. She hoped Najma would win the big race held near her village each year.

Every day, Lama trained Najma hard. She made Najma run fast again and again. She did not give her much rest. She only cared about building speed.

Before long, all that hard training wore Najma out. She stopped eating well. She no longer wanted to run, no matter how much Lama urged her on.

Lama's grandpa, Saleh, noticed this. He sat down beside her to talk. He said that speed alone does not make a true champion. He said Najma also needed patience and good care to race well.

Lama listened to her grandpa's words, even though it was hard to slow down. She began giving Najma good food and plenty of rest. She trained her slow and gentle, with real patience instead of rushing.

Before long, Najma felt strong and healthy again. She began to trust Lama more than ever. She followed her lead eagerly.

On the day of the race, Najma ran better than she ever had. She was fast and strong and full of energy. Lama finally understood that patience and care, not only speed, are what truly make a champion.

versions.title: The Camel Race Champion
versions.text:
Lama's family had raised racing camels for many years. They followed traditional ways passed down from her grandpa. She had a young camel of her own named Najma. She hoped Najma would win the region's biggest traditional race.

Every day after school, Lama trained Najma hard. She made Najma run fast again and again. She did not give her much rest. She believed speed was the only thing that mattered for a future champion.

Before long, all that hard training wore Najma out. She stopped eating well. She seemed to lose much of her stamina. She no longer wanted to run, no matter how much Lama urged her forward.

Lama's grandpa, Saleh, had trained camels for most of his life. He noticed this and sat beside her one evening to talk. He gently explained that raw speed alone does not create a true champion. A camel like Najma also needed patience, rest, and proper daily care.

Lama took his advice to heart. She began to groom Najma each morning and feed her well. She let her rest fully between each gentle session, building the camel's stamina slowly.

Within a few weeks, Najma felt strong and healthy again. She began to trust Lama more than ever, following her lead eagerly.

On the day of the race, Najma ran better than she ever had, showing both speed and stamina. Lama finally understood what her grandpa had meant: patience and steady, traditional care, not speed alone, make a true champion.

Lama's family had raised racing camels for many years. They followed traditional ways passed down carefully from her grandpa. She had a young camel of her own named Najma. She hoped Najma would someday win the region's biggest traditional race.

Every afternoon after school, Lama trained Najma hard on the open sand. She made Najma run fast again and again. She did not give her much rest. She firmly believed speed was the only thing that mattered for a future champion.

Before long, all that hard training wore Najma out completely. She stopped eating well. She seemed to lose much of her natural stamina. She no longer wanted to run, no matter how eagerly Lama urged her forward each day.

Lama's grandpa, Saleh, had trained camels for most of his long life. He noticed what was happening to the young camel. He sat down beside Lama one evening to talk things through. He gently explained that raw speed alone does not create a true champion. A camel like Najma also needed patience, plenty of rest, and proper daily care.

Taking his advice seriously, Lama changed how she trained Najma from that day forward. She began grooming her carefully each morning and feeding her well. She let her rest fully between each gentle session, slowly building the camel's stamina instead of pushing for it all at once.

Within a few weeks, Najma felt strong and healthy again. She visibly began to trust Lama more than ever, following her lead eagerly near the farm.

On the day of the race, with family and neighbors gathered to watch, Najma ran better than she ever had, showing both speed and stamina across the long course. Lama finally understood what her grandpa had meant: patience and steady, traditional care, not speed alone, are what truly make a champion.

versions.title: The Camel Race Champion
versions.text:
Lama's family had raised racing camels for many generations, following traditional ways passed down carefully from her grandpa, and she now had a young camel of her own named Najma, whom she hoped would someday win the region's largest traditional race, held every year on the edge of her village along a demanding, arduous desert course that tested every competitor's endurance to its absolute limit. Every afternoon after school, Lama trained Najma hard on the open sand near her family's farm, making her run fast again and again, without much rest, because she firmly believed, somewhat mistakenly, that raw speed was the only thing that mattered for a future champion.

Before long, all that relentless training wore Najma out completely: she stopped eating well, seemed to lose much of her natural endurance, and no longer wanted to run, no matter how eagerly Lama urged her forward each afternoon, until Lama began to worry seriously that something was wrong with her camel. Noticing what was happening, Lama's grandpa, Saleh, who had trained racing camels for most of his long life and had developed a sharp instinct for spotting a camel under strain, sat beside her one quiet evening to talk things through calmly and patiently, explaining that raw speed alone does not create a true champion and that a camel like Najma also needed patience, meticulous daily care, and enough rest to build lasting endurance, rather than being pushed too hard too quickly and carelessly.

Taking his advice seriously, Lama changed her training from that day forward, adopting a far more disciplined, meticulous routine than before: she began grooming Najma carefully each morning, feeding her well, and letting her rest fully between each gentle session, slowly and deliberately building the camel's endurance instead of pushing for speed all at once. Within a few weeks, Najma felt strong and healthy again, and a genuine rapport grew between girl and camel, as Najma began to trust Lama more than ever, following her lead almost instinctively each and every day on the training grounds.

On the day of the race, with family and neighbors gathered along the course to watch, Najma ran better than she ever had, showing both impressive speed and real endurance across the long desert track, and finishing strongly among the very fastest camels competing that day. Lama finally understood what her grandpa had meant all along: discipline, patience, and meticulous care, not speed alone, are what truly make a champion, a lesson she carried with her into every race that followed, long after that first difficult season had ended, and one she would, in time, pass down to her own grandchildren.

MID.prompt: Explain how Grandfather Saleh's advice changed the way Lama cared for Najma. Use at least two details from the article.

MID.modelAnswer: Grandfather Saleh's advice changed how Lama trained Najma in several ways. Before, Lama trained Najma hard every day without much rest, which made Najma tired and unwilling to eat. After her grandfather explained that patience and proper care matter as much as speed, Lama began grooming Najma, feeding her well, and letting her rest between gentle training sessions. Because of this change, Najma regained her strength and ran her best at the regional race.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a winning racing camel is simply born fast, and training cannot change that. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that a winning racing camel is simply born fast. In the article, Najma actually performed worse when Lama pushed her hard for speed alone, losing her appetite and endurance. Only after Lama adopted a disciplined, meticulous routine of grooming, feeding, and rest did Najma regain her strength and perform excellently at the race. Someone might argue that natural speed still matters, and the article does not deny that, but it shows clearly that patient, proper care was what finally allowed Najma's ability to show itself on race day.
